head.title: XSLT Debugger and Profiler for VS Code

meta.name: description
meta.content: How to debug XSLT with breakpoints and stepping into XPath, use print debugging, and profile a stylesheet to find its slow templates - in Visual Studio Code with Saxon.

div.p: When a transformation gives the wrong result, the question is always the same: what did the stylesheet actually do with this input? XSLT is declarative, so the answer isn't a line of code that ran first - it is which templates matched, what the variables held, and what each XPath expression returned. Debugging XSLT means being able to see those things.

img.alt: The XSLT debugger in Visual Studio Code, stopped at a breakpoint, showing the variables, context item and an XPath watch for the running stylesheet

figure.figcaption: Stopped at a breakpoint: the context item and variables, an XPath expression being watched, and the call stack of templates.

div.p: The extension's debugger runs a stylesheet with Saxon and stops at breakpoints you set in it. It shows the variables in scope, the context item with its position and size, and the call stack of templates and functions. You can step into, over and out of code - including inside a multi-line XPath expression - and step back or reverse-continue to see how you got there. Breakpoints can be conditional or use hit counts, and logpoints write values without stopping.

The values you want are easy to ask for: add an XPath expression to the Watch view or evaluate one in the Debug Console, and see the result as nodes, not just text. The output a stylesheet writes is mapped back to the XSLT that wrote it.

Sometimes the quickest tool is a message. The extension completes xsl:message instructions that write the variables in scope in color, and has functions for tracing a value inside an expression without changing its result.

img.alt: Print debugging output for an XSLT function: the items of a sequence shown with their paths, and a total

figure.figcaption: The items a function worked on, written to the terminal with their paths.

div.p: If a stylesheet is correct but slow, profile it. The profiler runs the stylesheet with Saxon timing each template, function and global variable, and shows them in a view, slowest first, with the time spent in each, how often it was called, and its share of the total. Click a row to go to the code, and the times are shown above each declaration in the editor. Profiling needs Saxon-PE or Saxon-EE.

img.alt: The profiler report for a stylesheet, listing its templates and functions with the share of the time each took

figure.figcaption: The profiler report: each template and function, with the share of the time it took.

div.p: The same debugger works for XSpec tests and for Schematron rules and assertions, so a failing test or a failed assertion leads straight to the code that caused it.
The details are in the user guide: the debugger, print debugging and the profiler.

div.h3: Can you debug XSLT in VS Code?
div.p: Yes. The XSLT/XPath extension provides a step-through debugger for XSLT, XSpec tests and Schematron, with breakpoints, stepping through multi-line XPath, step back, watch expressions and output mapped to the XSLT.
div.h3: How do I find slow templates in XSLT?
div.p: Profile the stylesheet. The profiler lists each template, function and global variable with its time, call count and share of the total. It needs Saxon-PE or Saxon-EE.
div.h3: How do I print a variable's value in XSLT?
div.p: Use xsl:message - the extension offers completions that write the variables in scope - or the tracing functions, which show a value inside an expression without changing the result.
Get the extension. Install XSLT/XPath for Visual Studio Code from the Marketplace.
